claim: Massive zygotic transcription begins in many organisms during the midblastula transition when the cell cycle of the dividing egg slows down.
source: Massive zygotic transcription begins in many organisms during the midblastula transition when the cell cycle of the dividing egg slows down.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established context for the study.

claim: A few genes are transcribed before the midblastula transition stage.
source: A few genes are transcribed before this stage but how this differential activation is accomplished is still an open question.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge.

claim: Massive recruitment of RNA polymerase II (Pol II) with widespread pausing occurs de novo during the midblastula transition.
source: We have performed ChIP-seq experiments on tightly staged Drosophila embryos and show that massive recruitment of RNA polymerase II (Pol II) with widespread pausing occurs de novo during the midblastula transition.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the ChIP-seq experiments performed in the study.

claim: Approximately 100 genes are strongly occupied by Pol II before the midblastula transition.
source: However, ∼100 genes are strongly occupied by Pol II before this timepoint and most of them do not show Pol II pausing, consistent with a requirement for rapid transcription during the fast nuclear cycles.
evidence: This is a finding from the ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Most pre-MBT genes do not show Pol II pausing.
source: However, ∼100 genes are strongly occupied by Pol II before this timepoint and most of them do not show Pol II pausing, consistent with a requirement for rapid transcription during the fast nuclear cycles.
evidence: This is a finding from the ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: The lack of Pol II pausing at pre-MBT genes is consistent with a requirement for rapid transcription during the fast nuclear cycles.
source: However, ∼100 genes are strongly occupied by Pol II before this timepoint and most of them do not show Pol II pausing, consistent with a requirement for rapid transcription during the fast nuclear cycles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on biological reasoning.

claim: The global change in Pol II pausing correlates with distinct core promoter elements.
source: This global change in Pol II pausing correlates with distinct core promoter elements and associates a TATA-enriched promoter with the rapid early transcription.
evidence: This is a finding from the promoter analysis performed in the study.

claim: A TATA-enriched promoter is associated with rapid early transcription.
source: This global change in Pol II pausing correlates with distinct core promoter elements and associates a TATA-enriched promoter with the rapid early transcription.
evidence: This is a finding from the promoter analysis performed in the study.

claim: Promoters are differentially used during the zygotic genome activation, presumably because they have distinct dynamic properties.
source: This suggests that promoters are differentially used during the zygotic genome activation, presumably because they have distinct dynamic properties.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the findings.

claim: In Drosophila, the MBT mainly occurs in the interphase of nuclear cycle 14, just before cellularization and subsequent gastrulation.
source: In Drosophila, the MBT mainly occurs in the interphase of nuclear cycle 14, just before cellularization and subsequent gastrulation (Foe et al., 1993), although there is some evidence that this may already occur in nuclear cycle 13 (Harrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is some evidence that the MBT may already occur in nuclear cycle 13.
source: In Drosophila, the MBT mainly occurs in the interphase of nuclear cycle 14, just before cellularization and subsequent gastrulation (Foe et al., 1993), although there is some evidence that this may already occur in nuclear cycle 13 (Harrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Before the MBT, a small fraction of genes may be transcribed as early as nuclear cycle 8.
source: Before the MBT, a small fraction of genes (De Renzis et al., 2007; ten Bosch et al., 2006) may be transcribed as early as nuclear cycle 8.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Unphosphorylated Pol II can be detected in nuclei from the earliest cleavage stages on, before the beginning of transcription.
source: Our immunostainings show that unphosphorylated Pol II can be detected in nuclei from the earliest cleavage stages on, thus before the beginning of transcription.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TBP can only be first detected during nuclear cycles 8–12, when significant transcription of pre-MBT genes occurs.
source: However, both TATA-box binding protein (TBP), the key subunit of TFIID, which binds to the promoter prior to Pol II recruitment, as well as Serine 5-phosphorylation of the C-terminal domain of Pol II (Ser5-P Pol II), which marks transcriptional initiation, can only be first detected during nuclear cycles 8–12, when significant transcription of pre-MBT genes occurs.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Serine 5-phosphorylation of the C-terminal domain of Pol II (Ser5-P Pol II) marks transcriptional initiation.
source: However, both TATA-box binding protein (TBP), the key subunit of TFIID, which binds to the promoter prior to Pol II recruitment, as well as Serine 5-phosphorylation of the C-terminal domain of Pol II (Ser5-P Pol II), which marks transcriptional initiation, can only be first detected during nuclear cycles 8–12, when significant transcription of pre-MBT genes occurs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ser5-P Pol II.

claim: Ser5-P Pol II can only be first detected during nuclear cycles 8–12, when significant transcription of pre-MBT genes occurs.
source: However, both TATA-box binding protein (TBP), the key subunit of TFIID, which binds to the promoter prior to Pol II recruitment, as well as Serine 5-phosphorylation of the C-terminal domain of Pol II (Ser5-P Pol II), which marks transcriptional initiation, can only be first detected during nuclear cycles 8–12, when significant transcription of pre-MBT genes occurs.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pol II is recruited to promoters de novo during the zygotic genome activation.
source: This was the first indication that Pol II is recruited to promoters de novo during the zygotic genome activation.
evidence: This is an inference from the immunostaining data.

claim: Pol II only occupies around a hundred genes before the MBT.
source: Despite the high Pol II signal in the pre-MBT sample, Pol II only occupies around a hundred genes before the MBT (Figure 1C, Supplementary file hosted by Dryad [7.6 Mb; Chen et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pre-MBT genes identified by ChIP-seq include previously described pre-MBT genes defined by in situ hybridization and microarray data.
source: These genes include previously described pre-MBT genes, as defined by in situ hybridization (ten Bosch et al., 2006) and microarray data (De Renzis et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous studies and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Pol II and TBP are recruited de novo to 4007 promoters during the MBT.
source: In contrast, Pol II and TBP are recruited de novo to 4007 promoters during the MBT, which equates to roughly a third of all genes (Figure 1C, Supplementary file hosted by Dryad [7.6 Mb]).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The recruitment of Pol II and TBP to 4007 promoters during the MBT equates to roughly a third of all genes.
source: In contrast, Pol II and TBP are recruited de novo to 4007 promoters during the MBT, which equates to roughly a third of all genes (Figure 1C, Supplementary file hosted by Dryad [7.6 Mb]).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the ChIP-seq data.

claim: 117 pre-MBT genes were identified as occupied by Pol II before the MBT.
source: This yielded 117 pre-MBT genes, many of which have known functions in sex determination, cellularization, anterio-posterior patterning and dorso-ventral patterning (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis with manual curation.

claim: Many pre-MBT genes have known functions in sex determination, cellularization, anterio-posterior patterning and dorso-ventral patterning.
source: This yielded 117 pre-MBT genes, many of which have known functions in sex determination, cellularization, anterio-posterior patterning and dorso-ventral patterning (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on functional annotation of the identified genes shown in Table 1.

claim: Among pre-MBT genes are 14 precursors of non-coding RNAs involved in maternal RNA degradation, dosage compensation, and RNA splicing.
source: Among them are also 14 precursors of non-coding RNAs, which are involved in maternal RNA degradation, dosage compensation, and RNA splicing, as well as many genes whose function is unknown but that are well conserved among insect species (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file hosted by Dryad [7.6 Mb]).
evidence: This is based on functional annotation of the identified genes.

claim: Many pre-MBT genes have unknown function but are well conserved among insect species.
source: Among them are also 14 precursors of non-coding RNAs, which are involved in maternal RNA degradation, dosage compensation, and RNA splicing, as well as many genes whose function is unknown but that are well conserved among insect species (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file hosted by Dryad [7.6 Mb]).
evidence: This is based on conservation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Most pre-MBT genes have no notable enrichment of Pol II at the pause site when they are initially transcribed.
source: Inspection of the Pol II occupancy revealed that most pre-MBT genes have no notable enrichment of Pol II at the pause site (+30–50 bp downstream from the transcription start site [Zeitlinger et al., 2007]) when they are initially transcribed, while TBP occupancy is found upstream (on average −20 bp from the transcription start site) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TBP occupancy is found upstream of the transcription start site (on average −20 bp) at pre-MBT genes.
source: Inspection of the Pol II occupancy revealed that most pre-MBT genes have no notable enrichment of Pol II at the pause site (+30–50 bp downstream from the transcription start site [Zeitlinger et al., 2007]) when they are initially transcribed, while TBP occupancy is found upstream (on average −20 bp from the transcription start site) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pre-MBT genes are much less paused than MBT genes when quantifying the degree of pausing with the pausing index.
source: When quantifying the degree of pausing with the pausing index (see 'Materials and methods'), pre-MBT genes are indeed much less paused than MBT genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A small number of pre-MBT genes have a higher pausing index and may be paused.
source: However, a small number of pre-MBT genes have a higher pausing index, lack enrichment of Pol II within the gene body and thus may be paused.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Pre-MBT genes can be classified into three distinct groups based on their Pol II occupancy during development.
source: We then classified the pre-MBT genes based on their Pol II occupancy during development and identified three distinct groups (Figure 2B,C, Supplementary file hosted by Dryad [7.6 Mb]).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Pre-MBT not-paused genes (n = 77) have highest expression during cellularization (nuclear cycle 14) and tend to diminish in expression thereafter.
source: Genes in the first group ('pre-MBT not-paused', n = 77) have highest expression during cellularization (nuclear cycle 14) and tend to diminish in expression thereafter (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pre-MBT not-paused genes appear never to become paused during early development.
source: These genes appear never to become paused during early development (see SNCF and the average profile in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pre-MBT dual genes (n = 30) initially show little evidence of pausing but higher levels of Pol II gradually accumulate at the pause site during and after the MBT.
source: Genes in the second group ('pre-MBT dual', n = 30) initially show little evidence of pausing; however, higher levels of Pol II gradually accumulate at the pause site during and after the MBT (see ac and the average profile in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pre-MBT paused genes (n = 10) appear to have Pol II that is paused or non-productive even at the pre-MBT stages.
source: Finally, there is a small group of genes ('pre-MBT paused', n = 10) that appear to have Pol II that is paused or non-productive even at the pre-MBT stages (see sim and the average profile in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pre-MBT paused genes have transcript levels that rise much later during pre-MBT stages compared to the first two groups.
source: This is consistent with the expression of these genes; their transcript levels rise much later during pre-MBT stages as compared to the first two groups (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pol II pausing exists during pre-MBT stages but most genes are non-paused.
source: This suggests that Pol II pausing exists during pre-MBT stages but that most genes are non-paused.
evidence: This is an inference from the ChIP-seq and expression data.

claim: MBT-maternal genes (3163 genes) are enriched for broadly expressed housekeeping genes.
source: We first subtracted from them the 3163 genes that are also maternally expressed ('MBT-maternal genes') because they are known to be enriched for broadly expressed housekeeping genes (Rach et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MBT-zygotic genes (844 genes) frequently have high Pol II occupancy at the pausing site and a high pausing index.
source: The remaining 844 genes ('MBT-zygotic genes') frequently have high Pol II occupancy at the pausing site and a high pausing index (Figure 3), suggesting that Pol II pausing is widespread during the MBT.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Pol II pausing is widespread during the MBT.
source: The remaining 844 genes ('MBT-zygotic genes') frequently have high Pol II occupancy at the pausing site and a high pausing index (Figure 3), suggesting that Pol II pausing is widespread during the MBT.
evidence: This is an inference from the ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: 251 MBT-zygotic genes (30%) are expressed at significant levels during late nuclear cycle 14 (MBT active genes).
source: When we analyzed the expression of these MBT-zygotic genes (Lott et al., 2011), we found that 251 genes (30%) are expressed at significant levels during late nuclear cycle 14 ('MBT active genes', see brk and the average profile in Figure 3A), while the remaining 593 genes ('MBT poised genes', see Dr and the average profile in Figure 3A) are expressed at very low levels typical for paused genes poised for activation (Zeitlinger et al., 2007; Adelman and Lis, 2012).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data analysis.

claim: 593 MBT-zygotic genes (MBT poised genes) are expressed at very low levels typical for paused genes poised for activation.
source: When we analyzed the expression of these MBT-zygotic genes (Lott et al., 2011), we found that 251 genes (30%) are expressed at significant levels during late nuclear cycle 14 ('MBT active genes', see brk and the average profile in Figure 3A), while the remaining 593 genes ('MBT poised genes', see Dr and the average profile in Figure 3A) are expressed at very low levels typical for paused genes poised for activation (Zeitlinger et al., 2007; Adelman and Lis, 2012).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data analysis and supported by citations.

claim: MBT active genes are expressed very early, while MBT poised genes tend to be first detected at later embryonic stages (stages 9–10 or later).
source: This difference in expression was confirmed by analyzing their in situ hybridization patterns: while the MBT active genes are expressed very early, the MBT poised genes tend to be first detected at later embryonic stages (stages 9–10 or later) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Many genes become newly paused during the MBT and are poised for later activation.
source: Thus, many genes become newly paused during the MBT and are poised for later activation.
evidence: This is an inference from the ChIP-seq and expression data.

claim: The significant difference in Pol II pausing between pre-MBT and MBT genes is likely to be biologically meaningful.
source: The significant difference seen in Pol II pausing between pre-MBT and MBT genes is likely to be biologically meaningful.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: Genes expressed before the MBT have to be transcribed particularly fast because the nuclear cycle is extremely short.
source: Genes expressed before the MBT have to be transcribed particularly fast because the nuclear cycle is extremely short (8 min in nuclear cycle 10, increasing to 13 min in nuclear cycle 12 [Foe et al., 1993]) and progression through mitosis causes abortion of nascent transcripts (Rothe et al., 1992; Shermoen and O'Farrell, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The nuclear cycle is 8 min in nuclear cycle 10, increasing to 13 min in nuclear cycle 12.
source: Genes expressed before the MBT have to be transcribed particularly fast because the nuclear cycle is extremely short (8 min in nuclear cycle 10, increasing to 13 min in nuclear cycle 12 [Foe et al., 1993]) and progression through mitosis causes abortion of nascent transcripts (Rothe et al., 1992; Shermoen and O'Farrell, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Progression through mitosis causes abortion of nascent transcripts.
source: Genes expressed before the MBT have to be transcribed particularly fast because the nuclear cycle is extremely short (8 min in nuclear cycle 10, increasing to 13 min in nuclear cycle 12 [Foe et al., 1993]) and progression through mitosis causes abortion of nascent transcripts (Rothe et al., 1992; Shermoen and O'Farrell, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pre-MBT genes are particularly short (median of 1228 bp vs 6024 bp for MBT-zygotic genes).
source: As previously noted (De Renzis et al., 2007), we also found that the pre-MBT genes are particularly short (median of 1228 bp vs 6024 bp, Mann–Whitney test p<10−20) and more often intronless (54.6% vs 9.2%, Fisher test p<10−23) compared to MBT-zygotic genes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene structure with statistical testing.

claim: Pre-MBT genes are more often intronless (54.6% vs 9.2% for MBT-zygotic genes).
source: As previously noted (De Renzis et al., 2007), we also found that the pre-MBT genes are particularly short (median of 1228 bp vs 6024 bp, Mann–Whitney test p<10−20) and more often intronless (54.6% vs 9.2%, Fisher test p<10−23) compared to MBT-zygotic genes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene structure with statistical testing.

claim: Pre-MBT genes frequently use the transcription start site that yields the shortest transcript (62.9% vs 30.6% for MBT-zygotic genes).
source: We also noticed that pre-MBT genes frequently use the transcription start site that yields the shortest transcript (62.9% vs 30.6%, Fisher test p<0.0003) (Table 2, and examples in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcription start site usage with statistical testing.

claim: The structural features of pre-MBT genes support the idea that rapid transcription is important during the fast cleavage cycles before the MBT.
source: This supports the idea that rapid transcription is important during the fast cleavage cycles before the MBT and makes it plausible that the lack of Pol II pausing is advantageous for pre-MBT transcription.
evidence: This is an inference from the gene structure analysis.

claim: The lack of Pol II pausing is advantageous for pre-MBT transcription.
source: This supports the idea that rapid transcription is important during the fast cleavage cycles before the MBT and makes it plausible that the lack of Pol II pausing is advantageous for pre-MBT transcription.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data.

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 are present in embryonic stem cells.
source: Histone modifications such as H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 are present in embryonic stem cells (Bernstein et al., 2006), in human sperm (Hammoud et al., 2009), and may be present in zebrafish embryos before gene activation (Vastenhouw et al., 2010; Lindeman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 are present in human sperm.
source: Histone modifications such as H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 are present in embryonic stem cells (Bernstein et al., 2006), in human sperm (Hammoud et al., 2009), and may be present in zebrafish embryos before gene activation (Vastenhouw et al., 2010; Lindeman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 may be present in zebrafish embryos before gene activation.
source: Histone modifications such as H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 are present in embryonic stem cells (Bernstein et al., 2006), in human sperm (Hammoud et al., 2009), and may be present in zebrafish embryos before gene activation (Vastenhouw et al., 2010; Lindeman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 were not found in Drosophila nuclei prior to gene activation.
source: However, we did not find these marks in Drosophila nuclei prior to gene activation.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and ChIP-seq data.

claim: H3K4me3 signal only starts to be detectable during the MBT in both immunostainings and ChIP-seq data.
source: In both immunostainings and ChIP-seq data, the signal of H3K4me3, a modification associated with gene activation, only starts to be detectable during the MBT (Figure 4A, see also the ChIP-seq results in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 1C.

claim: H3K27me3 can be detected in nuclei and in polar bodies at the earliest cleavage stages but is then undetectable in somatic nuclei until after the MBT.
source: H3K27me3, a marker of Polycomb-mediated gene silencing and possibly epigenetic memory, can be detected in nuclei and in polar bodies at the earliest cleavage stages but is then undetectable in somatic nuclei until after the MBT (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ChIP-seq H3K27me3 signal at Polycomb response elements (PREs) increases over time.
source: Consistent with this, the ChIP-seq H3k27me3 signal at Polycomb response elements (PREs) increases over time (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: H3K27me3 is likely present in oocytes but may be diluted or erased during replication.
source: Thus, H3K27me3 is likely present in oocytes but may be diluted or erased during replication consistent with a recent study (Petruk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the data and supported by a citation.

claim: It is unlikely that H3K4me3 or H3K27me3 have a direct role in regulating the zygotic genome activation in Drosophila.
source: Accordingly, it seems unlikely that H3K4me3 or H3K27me27 have a direct role in regulating the zygotic genome activation in Drosophila.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: Pre-MBT genes tend to have particularly low levels of H3K4me3.
source: We also noticed that pre-MBT genes tend to have particularly low levels of H3K4me3 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Even when pre-MBT genes continue to be transcribed during the MBT, H3K4me3 tends to be low and to accumulate to highest levels at further downstream nucleosomes.
source: Even when pre-MBT genes continue to be transcribed during the MBT, H3K4me3 tends to be low and to accumulate to highest levels at further downstream nucleosomes at pre-MBT genes.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MBT-maternal genes have a sharp peak of H3K4me3 at the +1 nucleosome.
source: This is in stark contrast to the MBT-maternal group, which has a sharp peak of H3K4me3 at the +1 nucleosome.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The difference in H3K4me3 levels between pre-MBT and MBT-maternal genes cannot be explained by lower levels of nucleosomes.
source: This difference cannot be explained by lower levels of nucleosomes since the nucleosome occupancy based on our Micrococcal Nuclease experiments coupled to deep sequencing (MNase-seq) does not show a dramatic difference between the two gene groups (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on MNase-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Histone modification levels tend to be dependent on the promoter types.
source: Since histone modification levels tend to be dependent on the promoter types (Rach et al., 2011), we next analyzed whether pre-MBT genes are enriched for specific core promoter elements.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MBT-maternal genes are strongly enriched for core promoter elements associated with dispersed initiation: Ohler1, Ohler6, Ohler7 and DRE.
source: Consistently, we found that MBT-maternal genes are strongly enriched for core promoter elements associated with dispersed initiation: Ohler1, Ohler6, Ohler7 and Dref response element (DRE) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on promoter motif analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Core promoter elements associated with focused initiation such as Inr, DPE, MTE and PB have previously been associated with paused genes.
source: Core promoter elements associated with focused initiation such as Initiator (Inr), downstream promoter element (DPE), Motif Two Element (MTE) and Pause Button (PB) have previously been associated with paused genes (Hendrix et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MBT-zygotic genes are highly enriched for Inr, DPE, MTE, PB and GAGA.
source: As expected, MBT-zygotic genes are highly enriched for these elements, as well as GAGA, which is consistent with reports that GAGA factor (GAF) promotes the recruitment of paused Pol II (Lee et al., 1992; Leibovitch et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on promoter motif analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GAGA factor (GAF) promotes the recruitment of paused Pol II.
source: As expected, MBT-zygotic genes are highly enriched for these elements, as well as GAGA, which is consistent with reports that GAGA factor (GAF) promotes the recruitment of paused Pol II (Lee et al., 1992; Leibovitch et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MBT-zygotic genes are not significantly enriched for the TATA box, although they are usually occupied by TBP.
source: We noticed that these genes are not significantly enriched for the TATA box, although they are usually occupied by TBP (Figure 1C, and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on promoter motif analysis and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The promoters of pre-MBT genes are significantly enriched for TATA.
source: In contrast, the promoters of pre-MBT genes are significantly enriched for TATA (Figure 5A, Supplementary file hosted by Dryad [7.6 Mb]).
evidence: This is based on promoter motif analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Only pre-MBT genes that initially show the non-paused profile (pre-MBT not-paused, pre-MBT dual) are significantly enriched for Inr and TATA.
source: Interestingly, only pre-MBT genes that initially show the non-paused profile (pre-MBT not-paused, pre-MBT dual) are significantly enriched for Inr and TATA.
evidence: This is based on promoter motif analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Only pre-MBT genes that are paused at some point (pre-MBT dual, pre-MBT paused) show enrichment for GAGA, Inr and PB.
source: Furthermore, only pre-MBT genes that are paused at some point (pre-MBT dual, pre-MBT paused) show enrichment for GAGA, Inr and PB (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on promoter motif analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The presence of specific core promoter elements correlates well with the Pol II occupancy profile across the gene body.
source: Thus, the presence of specific core promoter elements correlates well with the Pol II occupancy profile across the gene body.
evidence: This is an inference from the promoter motif and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The transcription factor Zelda and its binding motif (TAGteam motif) regulates the onset of zygotic gene expression.
source: Previous studies have shown that the transcription factor Zelda and its binding motif (known as the TAGteam motif) regulates the onset of zygotic gene expression (De Renzis et al., 2007; Harrison et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2008; ten Bosch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The binding levels of Zelda in the promoter region correlate well with the onset of gene expression.
source: Notably, the binding levels of Zelda in the promoter region correlate well with the onset of gene expression, although Zelda is also abundantly found at enhancers (Harrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Zelda motifs are highly enriched in the promoter region of pre-MBT genes.
source: Consistent with this, we found that Zelda motifs are highly enriched in the promoter region of pre-MBT genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on promoter motif analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enrichment of Zelda motifs is found in all three pre-MBT classes and does not correlate with the Pol II pausing pattern.
source: However, this enrichment is found in all three pre-MBT classes and does not correlate with the Pol II pausing pattern (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on promoter motif analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For pre-MBT stage non-paused genes, the top two motifs identified by de novo motif analysis were Zelda and TATA.
source: For pre-MBT stage non-paused genes (pre-MBT not-paused, pre-MBT dual), the top two motifs were Zelda and TATA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on de novo motif analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For MBT active genes, the top two known motifs identified by de novo motif analysis were GAGA and a motif that resembles DPE, MTE and PB.
source: In contrast, the top two known motifs for the most comparable MBT group (MBT active genes, which are also early-expressed developmental genes), were GAGA and a motif that resembles DPE, MTE and PB (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on de novo motif analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Pre-MBT and MBT genes differ in their core promoter sequences.
source: This confirms that pre-MBT and MBT genes differ in their core promoter sequences.
evidence: This is an inference from the de novo motif analysis.

claim: Zelda, Inr and TATA significantly co-occur among all Pol II-bound genes (pre-MBT and MBT genes) but not among all annotated genes.
source: For example, Zelda, Inr and TATA significantly co-occur among all our Pol II-bound genes (pre-MBT and MBT genes) but not among all annotated genes, suggesting that these motifs preferentially function together during early development.
evidence: This is based on co-occurrence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Zelda, Inr and TATA preferentially function together during early development.
source: For example, Zelda, Inr and TATA significantly co-occur among all our Pol II-bound genes (pre-MBT and MBT genes) but not among all annotated genes, suggesting that these motifs preferentially function together during early development.
evidence: This is an inference from the co-occurrence analysis.

claim: Rapid pre-MBT transcription without Pol II pausing is mediated by Zelda bound close to a TATA-enriched promoter.
source: This suggests a model in which rapid pre-MBT transcription without Pol II pausing is mediated by Zelda bound close to a TATA-enriched promoter (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data.

claim: Paused Pol II is typically established through GAF during the MBT at promoters with pausing elements such as DPE, MTE or PB.
source: In contrast, paused Pol II is typically established through GAF during the MBT at promoters with pausing elements such as DPE, MTE or PB.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data.

claim: There are two principle modes by which zygotic genes are activated but genes may also have elements of both and show a dual behavior.
source: Thus, there are two principle modes by which zygotic genes are activated but genes may also have elements of both and show a dual behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data.

claim: Pre-MBT genes are required for very early developmental events such as sex determination or cellularization.
source: Presumably, these pre-MBT genes are required for very early developmental events such as sex determination (Erickson and Cline, 1993; Barbash and Cline, 1995) or cellularization (Schejter and Wieschaus, 1993; Pritchard and Schubiger, 1996), or may be involved in early patterning events that require feedback regulation over time (for example ftz [Edgar et al., 1986; Pritchard and Schubiger, 1996] or sna [De Renzis et al., 2006; Reeves et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pre-MBT genes may be involved in early patterning events that require feedback regulation over time.
source: Presumably, these pre-MBT genes are required for very early developmental events such as sex determination (Erickson and Cline, 1993; Barbash and Cline, 1995) or cellularization (Schejter and Wieschaus, 1993; Pritchard and Schubiger, 1996), or may be involved in early patterning events that require feedback regulation over time (for example ftz [Edgar et al., 1986; Pritchard and Schubiger, 1996] or sna [De Renzis et al., 2006; Reeves et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: While Pol II pausing is commonly found at developmental genes and may be advantageous for their precise and synchronous expression in response to localized extracellular signals, a different mode of transcription is used during pre-MBT stages.
source: Thus, while Pol II pausing is commonly found at developmental genes and may be advantageous for their precise and synchronous expression in response to localized extracellular signals (Boettiger and Levine, 2009), a different mode of transcription is used during pre-MBT stages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by a citation.

claim: It is likely that transcription is optimized to achieve high levels of transcripts in a very short time period during pre-MBT stages.
source: Due to the short nuclear cycles at this stage, it is likely that transcription is optimized to achieve high levels of transcripts in a very short time period.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: The TATA box is a strong core promoter element that efficiently supports transcription in vitro.
source: TATA is a strong core promoter element that efficiently supports transcription in vitro (Aso et al., 1994), mediates efficient re-initiation in vitro (Yean and Gralla, 1997, 1999), and its presence in vivo correlates with 'bursts' of transcription that produce many transcripts within a short time (Zenklusen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TATA mediates efficient re-initiation in vitro.
source: TATA is a strong core promoter element that efficiently supports transcription in vitro (Aso et al., 1994), mediates efficient re-initiation in vitro (Yean and Gralla, 1997, 1999), and its presence in vivo correlates with 'bursts' of transcription that produce many transcripts within a short time (Zenklusen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of TATA in vivo correlates with 'bursts' of transcription that produce many transcripts within a short time.
source: TATA is a strong core promoter element that efficiently supports transcription in vitro (Aso et al., 1994), mediates efficient re-initiation in vitro (Yean and Gralla, 1997, 1999), and its presence in vivo correlates with 'bursts' of transcription that produce many transcripts within a short time (Zenklusen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TATA promotes pTEFb activity, leading to more efficient elongation rates in vitro and in vivo.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that TATA promotes pTEFb activity, leading to more efficient elongation rates in vitro and in vivo (Amir-Zilberstein et al., 2007; Montanuy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TATA-enriched promoters and paused promoters have different transcription dynamics and serve different purposes during development.
source: This suggests that TATA-enriched promoters and paused promoters have different transcription dynamics and serve different purposes during development.
evidence: This is an inference from the data and literature.

claim: The difference between TATA-enriched promoters and paused promoters is particularly evident during the zygotic genome activation.
source: While this difference is particularly evident during the zygotic genome activation as reported here, we propose that this difference is general and also applies to later development.
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the study.

claim: The difference between TATA-enriched promoters and paused promoters is general and also applies to later development.
source: While this difference is particularly evident during the zygotic genome activation as reported here, we propose that this difference is general and also applies to later development.
evidence: This is a proposal/speculation based on the data.

claim: Many genes are induced during late stages of embryogenesis without prior Pol II pausing and these genes are also enriched in TATA during muscle development.
source: For example, we have analyzed promoters during muscle development and find that many genes are induced during late stages of embryogenesis without prior Pol II pausing and that these genes are also enriched in TATA (Gaertner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The combination of Inr and TATA represents a separate class of promoters that is often found among genes expressed in adult tissues.
source: Consistent with this, statistical analyses suggest that the combination of Inr and TATA represents a separate class of promoters that is often found among genes expressed in adult tissues (FitzGerald et al., 2006; Lenhard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The properties of TATA are not specific to Drosophila.
source: Since the properties of TATA are not specific to Drosophila, it is likely that differences among promoter types and their propensity for Pol II pausing are conserved across animals.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about TATA.

claim: Differences among promoter types and their propensity for Pol II pausing are likely conserved across animals.
source: Since the properties of TATA are not specific to Drosophila, it is likely that differences among promoter types and their propensity for Pol II pausing are conserved across animals.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and general knowledge.

claim: The initiated form of Pol II (serine-5-phosphorylation of the CTD repeats—Ser5-P), as well as TBP are only detectible in the nuclei of pre-MBT embryos when zygotic transcription begins.
source: Immunostainings of embryos during pre-blastoderm stages (nc 1–7), pre-MBT (nc 8–12) and MBT (nc 13–14) suggest that the initiated form of Pol II (serine-5-phosphorylation of the CTD repeats—Ser5-P), as well as TBP are only detectible in the nuclei (outlined by the Lam 0 in red) of pre-MBT embryos when zygotic transcription begins (scale = 20 μm).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pre-MBT genes are also significantly bound in the pre-MBT sample.
source: Pre-MBT genes are also significantly bound in the pre-MBT sample; MBT-maternal genes also have maternally provided transcripts in the early embryo (RPKM > 1 during nc 10); the remaining genes are MBT-zygotic genes.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MBT-maternal genes have maternally provided transcripts in the early embryo (RPKM > 1 during nc 10).
source: Pre-MBT genes are also significantly bound in the pre-MBT sample; MBT-maternal genes also have maternally provided transcripts in the early embryo (RPKM > 1 during nc 10); the remaining genes are MBT-zygotic genes.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data.

claim: Among MBT-zygotic genes, MBT active genes are expressed during the MBT (RPKM > 5 at nc 14D), while the transcript levels of MBT poised genes are below this threshold.
source: Among the latter group, MBT active genes are expressed during the MBT (RPKM > 5 at nc 14D), while the transcript levels of MBT poised genes are below this threshold.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data.

claim: Pol II is only bound to few pre-MBT genes before the MBT.
source: Note that Pol II is only bound to few pre-MBT genes before the MBT and that there is massive de novo recruitment of Pol II during the MBT.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is massive de novo recruitment of Pol II during the MBT.
source: Note that Pol II is only bound to few pre-MBT genes before the MBT and that there is massive de novo recruitment of Pol II during the MBT.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Paused genes are expressed at lower levels and tend to be induced later.
source: Median RNA-seq expression data (Lott et al., 2011) of the three pre-MBT groups and the two MBT groups shows that paused genes are expressed at lower levels and tend to be induced later.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pre-MBT not-paused genes have a non-paused Pol II profile since they do not show elevated Pol II levels at the pause site during pre-MBT and MBT stages.
source: Note that pre-MBT not-paused genes have a non-paused Pol II profile since they do not show elevated Pol II levels at the pause site during pre-MBT and MBT stages.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pre-MBT dual genes switch from an initial non-paused profile during pre-MBT stages to a paused profile during the MBT.
source: Pre-MBT dual genes switch from an initial non-paused profile during pre-MBT stages to a paused profile during the MBT.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pre-MBT paused genes appear to be paused even during pre-MBT stages.
source: Pre-MBT paused genes appear to be paused even during pre-MBT stages.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both MBT active and MBT poised genes show widespread Pol II pausing.
source: Examples and average normalized enrichment (as in Figure 2C) of Pol II occupancy (blue) and TBP occupancy (pink) for the MBT-zygotic genes that are significantly transcribed during MBT (MBT active) or not (MBT poised). Both groups show widespread Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MBT active genes are mostly expressed at stage 4–6 (peri-cellularization).
source: Analysis of large scale in situ hybridizations (ImaGO database, see 'Materials and methods') confirms the earlier initial expression of MBT active genes (mostly stage 4–6, peri-cellularization) and shows that many MBT poised genes are first transcribed at later stages of embryogenesis (mostly stage 9–10, post-gastrulation).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Many MBT poised genes are first transcribed at later stages of embryogenesis (mostly stage 9–10, post-gastrulation).
source: Analysis of large scale in situ hybridizations (ImaGO database, see 'Materials and methods') confirms the earlier initial expression of MBT active genes (mostly stage 4–6, peri-cellularization) and shows that many MBT poised genes are first transcribed at later stages of embryogenesis (mostly stage 9–10, post-gastrulation).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: H3K4me3 is not detectable in nuclei of embryos before MBT.
source: Lack of detectable H3K4me3 immunostaining in nuclei of embryos before MBT.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H3K27me3 is observed in nuclei and polar bodies (pb) of early pre-blastoderm nuclei but not during pre-MBT or MBT stages.
source: H3K27me3 is observed in nuclei and polar bodies (pb) of early pre-blastoderm nuclei but not during pre-MBT or MBT stages.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H3K27me3 first becomes detectable again in post-MBT embryos.
source: H3K27me3 first becomes detectable again in post-MBT embryos (scale = 20 μm).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H3K27me3 is absent during the MBT but the levels increase soon after.
source: ChIP-seq experiments also suggest that H3K27me3 is absent during the MBT but that the levels increase soon after. Shown is the average pattern of H3K27me3 signal over input surrounding 441 previously identified Polycomb response elements (PREs).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Despite high levels of Pol II occupancy, H3K4me3 average gene enrichments are low at pre-MBT genes.
source: Despite high levels of Pol II occupancy, H3K4me3 average gene enrichments are low at pre-MBT genes (top left).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MBT-maternal genes have high H3K4me3 enrichment that peaks ∼200 bp downstream of the TSS.
source: This is in contrast to MBT-maternal genes, which have high H3K4me3 enrichment that peaks ∼200 bp downstream of the TSS (bottom left).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The overall nucleosome occupancy shows more pronounced nucleosome positioning at MBT maternal genes but the overall nucleosome occupancy is not dramatically different between pre-MBT and MBT-maternal genes.
source: The overall nucleosome occupancy, as measured by MNase digestion, shows more pronounced nucleosome positioning at MBT maternal genes but the overall nucleosome occupancy is not dramatically different (compare top and bottom panels at the right).
evidence: This is based on MNase-seq data shown in Figure 4C.
